utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could I remind you the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and I think Mr. Djurdjic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Sadiku. I'm Veljko Djurdjic, member of the Defence team for the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic. Together with me today is Ms. Marie O'Leary, member of the Defence team. I would kindly ask you to tell me if you do not understand the question that I'm putting to you, I'll try to rephrase then so that you could give me answers to all my questions.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, you live together with your parents in Donje Zabare, the village of Donje Zabare, if I understand you correctly; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us who else lived in that house together with your parents and you.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my house it was me with my two parents, my brother, his wife, and the four children of my brother. There was also another brother who was not married, and he was also living with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, in 1999 how old were your brothers?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were your brothers older than you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are older than me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me what it was that your father did in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father worked in Mitrovica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me what his profession was or where he worked.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in a mine in Mitrovica. It's called Fosfot, that's the name of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me what your maternal grandmother's name and surname was.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her name was Nazi Ferhati.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did your mother's parents originally hail from?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My grandfather was from Cerona [phoen] and my mother was -- my grandmother was from Bajkura.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sadiku, am I right if I say that you do not speak or understand the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Mr. Halimi in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The lawyer Halimi, Mahmut Halimi?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I thought you were asking about my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know the lawyer Mahmut Halimi or do you know him now? He told us that he originally hailed from Donje Zabare.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I did not know him; however, I came to know him after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where his house is now in Donje Zabare?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know where his house is. My parents know where the house is, but I do not know where that house you're asking me is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your response had to do with 1999, right, all the people who lived in the same house with you; right?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat the question again please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When I asked you about all the people who lived in the same house with you, did that have to do with 1999?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you do in 1999, in the beginning of 1999 before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I had just graduated from the elementary school, the eighth grade. I had no opportunity to follow the school later, so at that time I was helping my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We probably have a translation problem. You completed elementary school considerably before 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elementary school, yes. I graduated from it in 1995/1996, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you please tell me your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1st of July, 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you start school on time?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was 6 years old when I entered the first grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That would mean 1984, right? Did you attend elementary school regularly?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you say that you finished school in 1995/1996?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that year, but I think that is the year. So I finished the eighth grade on that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what year you went to Albania?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I crossed the border into Albania on 12th May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How come you know it was exactly the 12th of May? How come you remember that specifically?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it because it is true. It is an accurate date. This was the day on which I crossed the border from Kosovo into Albania, it happened on 12th May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something. Was that the first time you ever went to Albania in your life?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true, that was the first time when I set foot on Albania for the first time, on 12th May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sadiku, could you tell me the following: From your birth up until the moment when you went to Albania, what are the places you went to outside the place where you were born?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was born, I had -- I have been only in Zhabar, I followed the school in Donje Zabare six years, then I went to Shipol where I attended the school for two years because the school in Zhabar was closed down due to absence of classes. Then I have also been in Mitrovica. I have not been anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sadiku, according to the report of the military hospital in Tirana on the 8th of May, 1999, you were hospitalised in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But that is an annex to your statement, and you had confirmed that the statement was correct. But let us do things in the right order, and we'll get to that too. Am I right when I say that you gave a statement to Kenneth Ekdahl, an investigator of the Tribunal, on the 23rd of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that on that occasion the statement was read out to you in the Albanian language by Tahiri Asllan, an interpreter who attended your interview?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that you signed each and every page of the statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that with your own signature you confirmed that your statement contains everything that you had said to the best of your knowledge and as you remember it?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sadiku, can you tell us whether you had any contact with the investigators of the Tribunal before you gave this statement?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I've not met them before this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for Kenneth Ekdahl, the investigator of the Tribunal, did you first see him when you gave your statement on the 23rd of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. We met for the first time in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sadiku, as for the investigator, Kenneth Ekdahl, you met up with him in August 1999, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that you met Kenneth Ekdahl in August 1999 and that it is not correct, or rather, that it's -- well, I'm not saying it's incorrect; but it wasn't the first time that you saw him in 2001, which is what you said to us a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is as follows: I met in 2001 with the gentleman you mentioned, and I've not met him before that year. In 1999 and 2000 I was in hospital, in Germany, so it was not possible for me to have met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, in paragraph 41 of your statement from 2006 you stated that you met up with Kenneth Ekdahl investigator on the 23rd of August, 1999, and that you gave him your medical documentation from Albania, and he photocopied all of that and gave it back to you.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. I met this person for the first time in 2001. He came to my family. I gave to him my declaration, I also supplied him with all the medical reports. I have not met him before that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I have to check the original version. Ms. Sadiku, in the original version, not only in the translation that I'm reading out from the Serbian translation, it says that you gave your medical documentation from Albania to the investigator on that date. Please tell me whether you talked to him before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That question has been answered. The witness says: No, I met him in 2001. The statement may give the year 1999, it may be that that's a mistake or it may be the witness has some explanation for that. But it's clear the statement says 1999, yet it says it in the context that she handed documents to the investigator, who then photocopied them and gave them back to her on the 27th of August, 2001. It seems very likely that there's a mistake in the year in the statement, because photocopying is not going to take two years. But do you see -- is there something else that you were pursuing or is it merely that 1999 is shown in the statement as the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to fresh the witness's memory with all of this, whether the investigator talked to her in 1999 or whether another investigator talked to her in 1999, because I am going to present the statement from 2001, the one that was given, and that's the only one here actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you can take it that the Chamber is aware that there is a date difference, 1999 to 2001, just as the Chamber is aware that there is a date difference over the admission of the patient into the military hospital in Tirana. But in that record it appears in doctor's patient notes, whereas the witness confirms that it was not then but on the 12th of May, 1999, that she first crossed the border into Albania. And she says she first saw the investigator, Mr. Ekdahl, in August of 2001. Perhaps you can move on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, you said that in Mitrovica people could move about rather freely while the OSCE was there. Can you tell us from when until when the OSCE was in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to apologise because I'm not very good with dates. I know that the OSCE was in Kosovo before the war started, but I cannot give you any date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sadiku. Tell me just what it is that you remember; and if you don't remember, just say so and we'll move on -- no, actually -- actually, you said that while the OSCE was there your brother had been abused by the Serbian police on the road to Mitrovica. Tell me, did you report that incident to the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't tell anybody about this. It was only my family and my cousin who knew about it, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where that spot was where the police had mistreated your brother?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was between the two Zhabar villages, the Upper and Lower Zhabar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you present while that happened?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present; however, when my brother came back, he told me what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Up until the 13th of April, 1999, were there any police in your village?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Up until the 13th of April, there were police forces only along the main road, not in the village. The first time they showed up in the village was on the 13th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 9 of your statement you mentioned that the police came in Pinzgauer vehicles. Could you please tell us what kind of vehicles were there -- were they?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were police vehicles, blue, dark blue colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please describe what that vehicle looked like.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They resembled a jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you in the house when the police came?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The truth is that on the 13th of April the houses were set on fire, and as soon as we saw that we left before the police came in the village. This was on the 13th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it means that you were not present there if you say that in your house the police fired a burst of gun-fire into the ground?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're asking me about, it is true that I heard that after I returned from Germany to Kosova from someone else. This is not something that I saw with my own eyes. This is something I heard from someone else, from several people who had been, at the time, in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sadiku, to speed things up, could you please tell us -- indicate all those things that you do not know because you were there which are your direct knowledge so that we can cut your examination short. Ms. Sadiku, do you know how many houses there were in your village in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 500, 600 houses. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that police entered your village on the 13th of April, but you left the house when the police was at the other end of the village; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. On the 13th of April, as soon as we saw that houses were being set on fire, we left; on the following day, the 14th of April, when we returned to our home, the police forced us to leave the house. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that you did not see the people that you mention in your statement, the people that you described as having been detained by the police at the other end of the village?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The police came to the other end of the village and you say that you left your house, yet in your statement it says that the police officers from the other end of the village made the people leave their houses, forced them out of their houses, but you yourself did not see that. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's not clear to me, your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see the police come to the other end of the village and force people out of their homes at that -- in that part of the village, did you see those people gather in the yard of the carpenter's shop? Did you see that yourself?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's kind of mixed up. What I said is that on the 13th of April the police expelled half of the village. We didn't wait for the police to come to our house. We left on our own. On the 14th, we returned to our house. It -- the weather was not good. And on that day, the 14th of April, the police came to our house and forced us out. I was part of the group that was in the field that you refer to, and this is what I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sadiku, in the statement that you gave in 2001 you say that in your house there were 80 people and that they were from the Tamnik part of Mitrovica. And in the statement that you gave in 2006 you supplement that statement, adding that there were people from Cirez too. How come that in 2001 you say that there were only people there from Tamnik and then you add in 2006 that there were also people from Cirez, not only from Tamnik?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier I wasn't asked about this, and I gave the figure when I was asked about these persons -- I wasn't asked where these persons were from; however, later when they put a clear question to me where they were from, I mentioned there were also people from Qirez, from Tamnik, and from Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But, Ms. Sadiku, the first time that I asked you this question -- the first that you were asked this question you said that they were from Tamnik, and then it was only in 2006 that you said there were not only people from Tamnik but there were also people from Cirez there. So the investigator asked you the first time where those people who were in your house had come from. So could you explain why this discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, earlier I wasn't asked specifically where these people came from. In 2006 when they asked me specifically about these persons, the number of them and where they were from, I provided them with an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have Exhibit D002-5109.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, do you recognise the uniform of the police officers who came into your village on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you please mark it.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the next page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not without losing the marking. There's been a mark put on this --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I just wanted to show to the Court that the witness was able to recognise the uniform. So could we please then tender this into evidence, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- we can go back ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm trying to hurry us along, Mr. Djurdjic, because I know that we've got to finish two witnesses today. The longer you spend on this witness, it will be shorter you have with the next witness, so we will keep moving as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00066, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, when you left your home on the 14th because the police had arrived, did you have enough time to get ready and to get some of your things?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not allowed to take anything to us. They told us we had five minutes to leave our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what were you wearing when you left your home?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: With clothes, everyday clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How were you able to understand what the police officers were saying, the police officers that came into your house?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to understand because my mother and my sister, Lutfije Sadiku, speak B/C/S very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So can I take it then that they interpreted to you what the police officers were saying?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where were your father and your brothers when the police came in, into your house?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father and my brothers remained in the mountain, whereas we returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where is this mountain in relation to your village?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not very far from our house, about 100 [as interpreted] kilometres, not further.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I believe there is an interpretation mistake here. Could you please repeat how far was this mountain from your village.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you left for the mountain on the 13th, how far were you from your home?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same distance, 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And those mountains, are they in the direction of the Vaganice village? I'm not sure what the exact name is.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in the direction of Kopriva.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me when you left the village, did you move in the direction of Mitrovica or in the direction Sipolje?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the direction of Shipol, between Shipol and Lower Zhabar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you then get to the road that leads to Srbica, Klina, and Pec?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We got to Shipol, Lushte, then Kline, then Skenderaj, and proceeded in the direction of Peje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The village of Ljuste is next to the main road, close to it?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Lushte is adjacent to Shipol, it's on the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far is it from the Donje Zabare village, Ljuste?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the distance in kilometres. To tell you the truth, it was the first time for me to go and to see all these places that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sadiku, did you know that in Donje Zabare there is a hospital?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the 14th of April, as you were leaving your village and going towards Ljuste, was there any gun-fire in the mountains around you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To tell you the truth, we were scared and we had no time to look around and to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened to your father and your brothers?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My eldest brother worked in the market as a salesman; my father worked in this factory, he retired later. So they did work in the house, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No. I meant as you were leaving the village and when the police forced you out, what were your father and your brothers doing, where were they?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we returned in our house on the 14th of April, my father and brothers didn't dare come in the house. They were scared because of the police. They remained in the mountain. We only intended to change our clothes and return to the mountain where we were, but that didn't happen because the police came and expelled us from our home. And at the time we were separated, we were not all together; my father, brothers on one side; and we others were on another side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, who went on towards Klina and Pec with you, which of your family members?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother, my two sisters, my brother's wife, four children of my brother, and 20 other persons who were staying as refugees with our family; however, in that group it wasn't only my family members. There were about 8.000 people from different places who were part of that convoy when we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell me, which of your family members came to the village of Zablace with you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother; my two sisters; my sister-in-law, and her four children; and my aunt, my uncle's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have Exhibit -- it's a Defence document, rather, D002-5111.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, this is the village of Zablace. Could you please mark the house where you were, where you found lodging.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really apologise. It's very difficult for me. It was the first time for me to visit that village, so I cannot pin-point it on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And am I right when I say that you stayed in the village for three weeks?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please show us the church on this map, the one that you mention in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, it's the village of Zablace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00067, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, there are some discrepancies between your statements regarding whether you left alone or not, the route that you took, but I'm not going to be asking you any questions about that. What I am interested in is the portion of your statement where you say in 2001 that because of the gun-fire nobody could approach you to assist you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did the gun-fire come from? Did you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. From the part where the church was, from the courtyard of the church, on my way to fetch potatoes I saw policemen in the courtyard of the church; and after I was hit, I saw that the bullets came from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But you said that the gun-fire went on for half an hour, so who was firing at whom?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I was hit by a bullet, I suddenly felt very warm. I had kind of fever. It was early in the morning, 8.00. I started to move a little bit, and when they saw that I was moving they started firing in my direction. My friends who were with me informed my family that I had been hit. They came to assist me, but it was impossible for them to do that because there was continuous gun-fire from these policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the statement of this witness dated the 23rd of August, 2001, that's D002-5023, that's the English version; and the Albanian version is D002-5046. So could we please move to page 5, that's in the English version, and page 6 in the Albanian version of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to read paragraphs 3 and 4 where it says: "I picked up the potatoes ..." Can you see it, ma'am, or do you want me to read it out for you? "After three weeks on the 6th of May, 1999, at 0800 hours I went out into the yard to bring some potatoes. "I picked up the potatoes just a couple of metres from the door. I took the potatoes and started to go back to the door. When I was just outside the door, I felt a pain in my back. I fell to the ground. I heard no shooting before I fell. When I had fallen to the ground, I felt even more pain and now I heard some shooting. "Lying on the ground I felt a big pain, and when I looked in my clothes I saw a big hole in front of my chest. I realised that it was an exit hole from a bullet. I had been hit in the middle of my back on the left-hand side. The exit hole was on my right-hand side just under my breast. "When I was lying on the ground I tried to move but I was not able to raise my upper part of the body, and I had to remain on the ground. I tried to move and drag myself into the with my arms but I could not. When the gunmen saw I was moving, they started to shoot heavily against me. Because of the shooting, which lasted for half an hour, no one in the house could help me. "I was screaming for help but no one could assist me from the house." You didn't mention anyone coming out with you, you didn't mention that anyone went away from you, and this is the first statement that you provided. And today you told us something else. Is your memory fresher in 2006 and today or was it fresher when you first gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is as follows: On the 6th of May I was hit on the spine. I was with my eight friends. I wasn't alone. When my friends saw that I was wounded, they phoned my family. Later on, my sisters Lutfije and Fikrije Sadiku came to help, but it was impossible for them to assist me for half an hour because there was this continuous gun-fire from the police. I have mentioned it before. I don't know why it isn't there, but this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say -- or rather, let us do it this way. How far was the church from the location where you were?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot describe the distance in kilometres, but it wasn't far. You could see whether something was moving, a person or something else; but I cannot tell you the distance in kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you look, as you went to fetch the potatoes, in the direction of the church, did you look in that direction at all?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my friends on our way to fetch potatoes, we noticed the police presence in the courtyard of the church. They had lit a fire early in the morning in the courtyard, and we could see that there were policemen there in the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you were injured, were you able to see the church?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Once we fetched the potatoes we set off in the direction of the house where we were staying. About 1 metre or so from the edge of the house, my friend asked me to swap because her hands were tired from carrying the potatoes. At that moment, as I was trying to pick up the potatoes, I had my back turned to the location where the police was and from where they were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I conclude that you did not see, since you had your back turned to the location, you could not see who actually fired the shots?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that at the time I was hit by a bullet I had my back turned to this location, where the police were. So once I was hit, I don't know how, but I turned towards the direction where the police were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were injured very badly and you were in different places for several days. As you were moving towards the border, you were on a tractor; am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were lying down, weren't you, in view of the injury that you had sustained?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Along the way, no one searched you; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one place we were searched by the police. They asked why I was lying on this tractor. My sister answered to the police, telling them that I was invalid from my birth, as was another person who was lying on that same tractor with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was whether I was right when I said that the police had not searched you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were not checked, searched by the police. On the way, however, they did ask for money and valuables, but they didn't body search us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that not a single one of your document was taken away from you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right. In Peje, the police stopped the convoy and collected all personal documentation from these people, IDs, passports, birth certificates, and so forth, in Peje, and they burnt them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You say that this was in Pec at the check-point. What about the border?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the border, before we crossed into Albania, they asked for money, for 500 Deutschemarks, and for valuables.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And they told you that they would not let you go unless you gave them the money they had asked for?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you gave 500 Deutschemark in order to be able to go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We gave them what we had. I don't know exactly how much we gave them, but we did give the money to be able to cross into Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Sadiku. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honours. I only have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, you were asked by my learned colleague about the day of the 13th of April when you left your house after having seen other houses of the village burning, and you went to the forest and stayed there for the night. I wanted to ask you: How did you leave, if you remember? By which means I mean.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left on foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you remember for how long you travelled to arrive to the forest?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: About one hour or one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And was it the same on your way back the following morning, on the 14th, when you returned to your village?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thanks for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you help me, please. When you went to the forest or the mountain with your family on the 13th of April, was your father with you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The two brothers that were living in the house, were they with you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We all spent that night in a tent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. The next morning you've told us you came back to get dry clothes and so forth. Your father and your two brothers, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father and my two brothers came half the way to the house. When they saw that the police was present in one part of the village, they didn't dare enter the village. They wanted to avoid the police because they knew what could happen to them once they meet the police. So they returned in the mountains whilst we proceeded towards my house to get the dry clothes and something to eat. And shortly after we arrived in the house, the police came and expelled us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You'll be pleased to know that completes the questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for your attendance here in The Hague again. We are very grateful for the assistance you've been able to give to us, and you are of course now free to go back to your family and your ordinary living. Thank you again for being prepared to assist. We will now adjourn for the first break and resume at 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would also like to thank you for giving me the opportunity to attend this Court for the second time. Whenever there is need for me to come and testify, I will be ready to come and testify to tell you the truth, as I did yesterday. I thank you very much for everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We know it's a special difficulty for you to cope with the problem of moving, and we are very grateful for your attendance. We adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next witness is waiting immediately outside the door and can be brought in. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The next witness is Mr. Branimir Aleksandric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please read aloud the affirmation which is now shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness, could you please start by stating your name and your current position.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: My name is Branimir Aleksandric. I'm a professor at the medical school of the University of Belgrade. The subject I teach is forensic medicine. I'm also the director of the Forensic Medicine Institute which is part of the medical faculty of the University of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Aleksandric, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution in June 2006?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to review this statement before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And while reviewing your statement, did you make a couple of corrections to the information contained in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm going to go very briefly through these corrections and ask you to confirm if the corrections as stated by me are accurate. Paragraph 1 in the middle of the paragraph there's a sentence that states that: Before the wars in the former Yugoslavia you taught as an associate professor of forensic medicine at the medical faculty in Sarajevo before 1992 and also at the medical faculty in Banja Luka during 1991 and 1992. Did you correct the years stated here and indicate in proofing that you taught as an associate professor of forensic medicine in Sarajevo in 1991 and 1992 and also taught at the medical faculty in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, this correction is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Paragraph 6, the third sentence currently states: "I caused the entire scene to be photographed before anything was touched ..." Did you correct this in proofing to state: "I caused the entire scene to be photographed and video-recorded before anything was touched ..."?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Other than for those two corrections, are you satisfied that the information contained in your statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this witness statement, this is 65 ter 02412 and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00507, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Aleksandric, did you also testify in October 2006 in the case of Milutinovic et al.?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review your transcript from that case?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Recently -- well, yesterday, yesterday, at your office at the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Having reviewed your transcript from the previous case, if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked then would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this transcript, this is 65 ter 05065, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00508, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I will now proceed to read the court summary of this witness's evidence. The witness is the head of the Belgrade Institute of Forensic Medicine. In 2002 the witness coordinated the work of a team of forensic experts working on burial sites discovered at the MUP firing range at Batajnica, Serbia. He describes the investigative methods used, including how the bodies and other evidence were exhumed and secured prior to examination, as well as the forensic examination process. He further describes the process by which samples of bones were taken from the bodies for DNA analysis and handed over to an ICMP representative in Belgrade. The witness identifies and authenticates copies of forensic reports produced for the graves coded Batajnica 3 and Batajnica 5. That is the end of the summary of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. I do wish to point out that the exhibits which are referred to in paragraph 16 of this witness statement and which were attached to our 92 bis motion have been agreed upon by the parties, and they're currently in evidence. Two of these exhibits, these are currently Exhibits P97 and P102 have no translations in e-court and this was noted by Your Honours in the decision on our 92 bis motion of forensic witnesses. We seek to withdraw these two exhibits. Although they're relevant to the issues in this case, we do not want to burden CLSS with the translation of these documents which are quite lengthy, and I note that these specific -- the specific reports which are contained within those exhibits do not relate directly to any of the scheduled victims. So we will be withdrawing those two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's your motion. Is there any objection, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think that these two documents are very important, even more so because the Office for Missing Persons and Forensic Medicine verified those findings, and their very own findings were absolutely contrary in relation to Batajnica 3 and Batajnica 5. Generally speaking, in relation to all the findings that were made by the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Belgrade. That is why I believe that it is very important that they should be part of the evidence admitted in this case. We will see later - I don't want to pre-empt matters - we'll see what the findings are of the Office for Missing Persons and Forensic Medicine as compared to the findings of the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Belgrade. If the time is right now, I would like to suggest that they be marked for identification, and then when the translations come, they be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They have actually been admitted in evidence and the Chamber has ordered that English translations be provided. That is the current situation, so as not to delay with the time - I don't know how long you'll be - but we, I think, should finish the evidence of the witness and then we -- if necessary, we can return to these two exhibits. That completes your examination-in-chief then, does it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to point out the exhibits which are referred to in paragraph 16 which are in evidence in addition to the two I mentioned it's Exhibits P98, P99, P100, P101, and P120. These are the exhibits that are referred to in paragraph 16. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the two that are in question are Exhibits P97 and P102. Yeah. Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. However, before the questions there is a mistake, or rather, there was a mistake and I believe that it has been corrected in relation to the English translation of some documents. I noted that -- please -- actually, it is stated here that there is no translation for 101, whereas there is a translation for that exhibit; and there is no translation of 102. I would like to draw your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I am Veljko Djurdjic, member of the Defence team of the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic; together with me is Ms. Marie O'Leary, member of our team. Mr. Dragoljub Djordjevic, lead counsel, is away on official business. You and I speak the same language. In order to make it possible for the court staff to do their jobs properly, please wait for my question to be transcribed and then please give me your answer, and then I will wait for you, although you are already aware of that. Professor, you are a doctor of medicine, medical science. Could you please tell me what your actual field is.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Forensic medicine, forensic pathology, whatever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us the following: After you graduated from the Faculty of Medicine, how did your professional career evolve?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: All of that is contained in the statement that I gave 2006. If necessary, I'll repeat all of it. Just tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No. I would just like to know how much time you needed to become a specialist in forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: At that time, it took four years. I believe that's how long it lasted at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And before that you had to do the compulsory internship, and then only could you start your specialisation in forensic medicine; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: First of all, it is compulsory to work as an intern for a year and then a two-year clinical residency or some other kind of residency. Mine was at the Institute for Anatomy and as a general practitioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. When were you put on the list of permanent forensic experts?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Where? In the country?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: In 1993 I believe or 1994, but I think it was 1993; and this was a decision made by the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you on the list of forensic experts outside Serbia too?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What were the requirements that you had to meet in order to become a permanent forensic expert?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, appropriate professional qualifications, primarily the residence -- the specialisation, rather, and the experience involving some serious court cases. And by -- when I say "professional experience," I mean providing expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do I understand it correctly that you are also a member of the Forensic Medicine Board of the medical school in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have been a member since 1996. This is when I was appointed the secretary of the board; and since 2006, I have been the chairman of the board. This is a board that consists of members who are appointed by the council of the medical school from among the prominent practitioners in their field and people who have already proven their good-quality work in various court cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what is the function of the Forensic Medicine Board?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: The Forensic Medicine Board provides expert reports, at the request of the courts, of highly complex cases. In most cases, these are the cases where there are conflicting expert reports that are already presented and the experts in question were unable to come to an agreement. In some cases, particularly when malpractice is in question, this board provides expert opinions even before other expert reports were provided. So in those cases it is the first-instance body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So can we conclude that the Forensic Medicine Board is a body that provides super expertise in medical field?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Professor, you headed the team that performed the exhumations at the Batajnica 3 and 5 sites, and in your statement you explained the procedure that you applied. I would now like to ask you this: Is this the procedure that is stipulated by the medical science -- the procedure that involves the exhumation and then the autopsy or post mortem examinations?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: First of all, I did not participate only in the inquiries into the Batajnica 3 and 5 sites. The -- it was actually Professor Dunjic who started investigating the Batajnica site in 2001, and he dealt with two graves there. We picked up where he left off, and we continued to inspect the area, the site. And we assigned numbers to subsequent sites, 3 through 8. So it's not only 3 and 5. On the other hand, the methodology that we applied in our work is the methodology that is generally accepted. The reason why it is accepted is because it is based on the experience, both in our country and abroad, when it comes to dealing with mass graves and execution sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain to us the role of forensic anthropologists in your team. You had a forensic anthropologist on your team.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: First of all, the team that does this work has to involve experts of various -- from various domains; and in 2002 when I took over the Batajnica case, I insisted on it. And that is why we involved also the anthropologists. Anthropologists are very important in this joint effort, especially when it comes to bodies that are fully disarticulated and full report of an anthropologist who has dealt with the bones. The findings of an anthropologist assist the pathologist, the forensic medicine experts, to provide their final opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your work, were there any foreign observers or representatives of the Tribunal or the OTP?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a number of observers who were there almost on a daily basis. There was nothing clandestine about our work. We did our work in public, and they could attend whenever they wished. The only thing I asked from them, since they usually came in large groups, was not to obstruct our work so that we don't waste any time because they took photographs and filmed the procedure. There were representatives of the embassies, of the NGOs, of the United Nations, the International Red Cross, the Missing Persons Commission. I don't want to list them all because it's all listed in the protocols anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you told that the missing persons and forensic medicine office carried out a forensic inspection of the findings of the autopsies carried out by the Forensic Medicine Institute from Belgrade at the Batajnica site? I'm now talking about the time when they did the verification, not at a later stage. Perhaps you heard about it here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I can't understand the question. Did I hear what?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you notified that the missing persons and forensic medicine office with KFOR in Pristina actually carried out forensic inspection of the autopsy reports provided by the forensic medicine institute in Belgrade at the Batajnica site?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your expert opinion, a forensic anthropologist, when he or she analyses the skeleton, determining the age, the sex, and the height, can they also determine the circumstances of the death of the person in question?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that the role of the anthropologist is important within the team-work and that their findings can assist the medical doctor who actually makes the final determination about the death of the person in question. So the anthropologist can only participant as members of a team, but it is the medical doctor who makes the final determination because he or she has the expert knowledge in medicine. Anthropologists know some medical elements, but they are not doctors. But just to give you an analogy, a psychologist and a psychiatrist. A psychologist can be a member of a team which is led by a medical doctor, a psychiatrist, but the psychologist cannot assume the role of a psychiatrist, who is a medical doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me what condition were the bodies in at the Batajnica 3 and 5 sites in terms of how badly decomposed they were?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: All the bodies were generally highly putrefied. The decomposed and destroyed part of the putrefaction process so that some of the remains were nothing but bare skeletons with very little remnants of the soft tissue around the bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you this: After you did your work and before you handed in all the skeletons that you had examined to -- back to Kosovo, did this process continue, or were they kept in such a state that they were no longer decomposing?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: After we autopsied the bodies, all the bodies were placed in some tunnels. I don't know what the tunnels were used before. They were next to the training area used by the SAJ, but at any rate those were tunnels dug into the ground and the temperature inside those tunnels was much lower than outside. But at any rate, in summertime the temperature in those tunnels was not as low as it is in refrigerators. So I can conclude that the process of decomposition continued for all intents and purposes. In other words, we did not have the refrigerators where you would typically put bodies in after we processed them, but we stored them in the tunnels.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why, in your reports for Batajnica 3 and 5 sites and in general for all the sites that the Forensic Medicine Institute processed, does it say that the cause of death cannot be determined for decomposed bodies?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the general principle. This is how you do work in forensic medicine. These are conclusions that only pertain to the findings obtained by the autopsy of the exhumed bodies. So this is the conclusion regarding those findings. Now, you can do an expert analysis later on, bearing in mind the circumstances, the autopsy itself, possibly determining the site where the bodies had been before. So from this kind of expert analysis one can get a more accurate conclusion about the most probable cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, I now have to bring you back in time a little bit. Based on only the reports on forensic analysis, is it possible to determine the mechanism how injuries were inflicted and the cause of death for bodies that are in advanced state of decomposition?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: When you have injuries to bone, in some cases they are quite peculiar when they're caused by a projectile or if you find the projectile itself then you're able to determine how the injury was inflicted, the mechanism itself, to determine in what direction the projectile was moving, whether the victim was facing the assailant or the muzzle or was -- had her or his back turned to it. So you can reconstruct the mechanism how the injury was inflicted at times; at other times you cannot do that. Sometimes you can do the most probable mechanism. And what was your next question, mechanism of injury, and what was the other thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, the cause of death solely on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Solely on the pre-autopsy examination of decomposed bodies, you cannot determine the cause of death. This is what I've already said. But later on when the expert learns not only of the results of the autopsy report but when he or she gathers all the other relevant data, the expert can conclude with a high degree of probability what the cause of death was or, alternatively, no such conclusions can be made. Let me give you an example. If the -- if it was determined that the round passed through the head, you can say that the most probable cause of death was a through-and-through wound to the head caused by a projectile of some sort. But if you don't have any elements that might lead you to such a conclusion, then cause of death remains unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what are the other elements, can you tell us that, the elements that make it possible for an expert witness to reach a conclusion as regards the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, the other elements, we're talking about the data that are obtained in the course of an inquiry or investigation. For instance, if you have a mass grave, that would be the site where the persons went missing, various witness statements. So from this data, you can obtain facts that might be linked with your autopsy report, and then this might lead you to determine the likeliest cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There are some views that your approach to the determination of the cause of death in the bodies that were found there at an advanced stage of decomposition is restrictive. Does science, forensic medicine, still support this position of the Forensic Medicine Institute or has something changed in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you, our conclusion about the cause of death pertains only to the autopsy that was performed on the exhumed decomposed bodies. At the initial stage of the investigation, it is absolutely restrictive; and this is why I insisted that we do this as a team and that's why we did it. In particular, the assistance of the anthropologist was important. And I've already told you, the anthropologist provides us with facts that we can then build into our medical domain, and anthropologists thus assist us to get at the most probable cause of death so it is no longer restrictive. That's what I told you. It might be restrictive when it comes to conclusions reached only on the basis of the autopsy of decomposed bodies; but afterwards, the expert analysis expounds and we can provide a more flexible conclusion. And the ultimate objective is to assist the court at the one hand to remove this initial restrictiveness and to assist the court in concluding whether any crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, if a body is already decayed and we establish that a person had been injured by use of a fire-arm, can we establish whether the person was alive or not once the fire-arm was used?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: In general terms, you cannot establish that. In order to establish that someone had been injured while he or she was still alive, there have to be some vital reactions on the body itself. If there are no such reactions on the body, and there aren't if the body is decomposed, nevertheless there may still be some traces that indicate to us that the person had been injured while still alive. However, when we give our final opinion, we establish what the most probable cause of death was; we do not say what the absolutely certain cause of death was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've said to us several times during expertise rather than autopsies and autopsy reports. Do you mean that this involves all the other elements that the expert has to be aware of in order to provide an expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: I repeat, we can say, as doctors, what the most probable cause of death was. In this we assist the Court; however, the Court deals with the rest of the evidence too in order to reach their final decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the bodies are well into the process of decay or decomposition, can it be established whether the persons lost their lives in a mutual armed conflict or whether they were defending themselves?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Again I don't understand your question. Mutual conflict -- it's one and the same thing, isn't it, defence or mutual conflict --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel has to pause before putting a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you must allow the professor to finish his answer before you start to put another question because the interpreters are moving through several languages, and they can't possibly keep up. And what was being said then was lost by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Professor, my mistake. Was there an armed conflict or were there some persons who were simply not in a position to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, only on the basis of the injuries sustained, it is hard to establish with any degree of certainty what had happened. Again, we can talk about a more probable way in which they had been injured, say from a shell or from a grenade. That can happen during an armed conflict too, but also this kind of injury can be sustained if somebody throws a grenade on -- or a shell on a group of people who get killed in that way. After all, that's what happened in Belgrade during the NATO bombing when so many civilians lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for some of the bodies that you examined, you and your team that is, did they have any military insignia?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: At the locality that was dealt with by my team, that is to say from localities 3 through 8, if I remember correctly there was one body with green camouflage trousers, so it was just one body. But, in a way, there were some combat markings there. There was a bandanna that was tied to the belt of the -- that was on the body, either on the left- or on the right-hand side. I know from what I had been told that the soldiers were told to tie ribbon or bandannas every day on their shoulders or on their belts so that they could tell who was who because basically everyone wore the same camouflage uniforms. On the other hand - I'm speaking from memory, I have not dealt with the entire material - but in terms of my general impression and as far as I can remember, about one-third of the bodies had military boots with metal in the soles. So if military boots are supposed to be something that soldiers wear, of course that doesn't have to mean in itself that somebody was indeed a soldier or not, but I'm saying that in about one-third of all cases, or perhaps even more, these boots were found with a metal insole in the sole of the boot, so such boots were worn as protection from booby-traps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I read your statement carefully; however, I did not notice that it contains what you said just now.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, it's all in the transcripts. If someone reads all the transcripts, then this can be read too in relation to the bodies concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: However, it's not in your statement given to the OTP. Have you informed the Prosecutors about what you stated just now and what is written in your transcripts?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Did I inform the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember whether they asked me. No one here in court asked me, and in the OTP -- well, I know that I discussed that too, but who, where, when, I can't remember exactly because I talked to the representatives of the OTP in Belgrade and at work and at the OTP office in Belgrade and here in The Hague. And on some occasion, as far as I can remember, I did talk about that as well; however, here in the courtroom, nobody really asked me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understand you correctly - correct me if I'm wrong - if one were to analyse your autopsy reports one could establish specifically what the number of persons was with this particular phenomenon of the military boots?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of autopsy reports, can it be established what the cause of death was in the case of a person who had drowned over two months ago and was in the water all the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: After spending two months in the water, can one distinguish on a corpse between blood and decomposition fluids?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, look, blood is the first to decay or decompose. And if decomposition fluid is in the blood vessels, that is decomposed blood. But to make a literal distinction between blood and this fluid is virtually impossible because everything decomposes and the blood is the first to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After two months' time, if an object is in water, can one observe the existence of blood?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: I do not understand what you're saying. On an object?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, an object that's in the water for two months, can one visually establish that there is blood there?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: With the naked eye?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: With the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: I have not had an opportunity to see that over the 30 years that I've been in this line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When corpses have been changed through decomposition, can one establish with certainty how far away a bullet had been fired?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: You cannot say anything with any degree of certainty in the case of a decomposed body. You can just talk about higher or greater probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Except in some special cases. For instance, exit/entry wounds in the skull, and when you reconstruct skull bones then you can see where the entrance was and where the exit was. And if the bullet was fired at very close range, then the entrance wound is much bigger and then you can say with a certain degree of certainty that the firing was at very close range. There are some cases that are even more specific; however, I would like to note that one cannot speak in general terms about all of this because in the procedure involved in this kind of expertise every case has a story of its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to repeat everything so that we don't waste any time. You explained to us what the process of expertise is and what the elements involved are. I'm asking you questions now only on the basis of the autopsy reports, whether something can be established on that basis, and also the things that were established in the autopsy reports. I'm not talking about expertise and other elements; I'm only talking about autopsy reports and findings. My next question, Professor, is that only on the basis of what an exit/entry wound looks like on tissue that had decomposed, that the canal of the wound can be established and can the calibre of the bullet be established, the bullet that had caused the wound?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: First of all, the calibre of the projectile is never established on the basis of the size of the exit or entry wound. The size of the entry wound depends on whether there was a right angle involved and whether it had lost a bit of its force, et cetera. As for the exit wound, it can be much bigger than usual because there are always these secondary projectiles. I mean, when a projectile passes through a body then it always takes bits of tissue along as well. So the exit wound doesn't have to be a single one. Say, if the projectile hits a bone, then there can be bone particles on the projectile as it leaves the body. But as I said, every case is different and tells a story of its own. As for the possibility of -- what was it that you were asking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about an advanced stage, skeletised -- when we're talking about skeletised body?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: In such cases if it is established, for instance, that bones had been injured rather than soft tissue and if one concludes that it was a projectile that caused these wounds, then on the basis of the direction, you can establish where the projectile came from, whether it came from the face or from the back or from the side in relation to the individual involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Only on the basis of the autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible. As I have already said, it is possible to establish the direction from which the projectile came, or rather, the mechanism that caused the injury on the basis of the bones themselves, the autopsy examination of the bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of the description in the autopsy report, can conclusions be drawn on the amount of time that a corpse had spent in the ground, in the soil?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: In general terms, no. In order to establish time of death, generally speaking, one has to be aware of the temperature conditions involved. And if you are dealing with bodies that were in this advanced stage of decomposition, it is virtually impossible, more than five months, more than ten months, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are forensic medical findings based on assumptions or facts?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
