utterances.text: I personally never rely on assumptions in forensic procedures, and I never use the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the province of work of a forensic anthropologist, does it mean that bone injuries are looked at too as well as the mechanism of their incurrence?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: The first two, yes, but as for cause of death I've already said that the findings of an anthropologist are of great assistance to the forensic doctor who is supposed to decide what the cause of death was. As I said, the anthropologist cannot interfere with the doctor's work, just as a psychologist cannot interfere with the work of a psychiatrist who is a medical doctor, again. But I repeat, the findings of an anthropologist are very important for the court because they are very important for the ultimate findings of the medical doctors involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible to determine the cause of death when we're talking about drowning in a well on the basis of solely macroscopic findings without any further analyses?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, if it is a fresh body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what would be considered as a fresh body in forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, a fresh body is a body that hasn't yet begun to decompose or putrefy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please tell me, how long does a body have to remain in water for the putrefaction to actually begin?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the temperature of the water, but one thing is for sure: The putrefaction process proceeds much quicker in summer than it does in winter. So again, you need to know the circumstances in order to be able to be as accurate as possible about the time of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, is it possible to draw any conclusions on the basis of injuries themselves as to whether they were inflicted by shrapnel or fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: It is possible to do so in fresh bodies. In putrefied bodies it is possible if we find the objects that caused the injury in the body itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Professor, thank you very much. I don't have any further questions for you. So thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Kravetz, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Aleksandric, you were asked some questions of whether you had observed any military insignia on the bodies that you examined, and you indicated what you had been able to observe. You referred to a green camouflage trousers and you also referred to boots. Would this information have been recorded for each body in the forensic reports that you prepared, the information on the clothing that you were able to find for the different remains?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, they were marked. Everything that was found on each body was described in detail and photographed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this would be under which heading in the report when you are referring to specific -- the clothing --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Under the heading clothes or clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Doctor, when the bodies in the mass graves at Batajnica were finally autopsied, what was the sum total of all the bodies, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't be accurate about the figure because I was called here to testify as a fact witness, not as an expert witness. I'm now talking off the top of my head. I did not prepare for the expert testimony. According to our analysis from 2002, there were at least 700 bodies, 703, 704, that's the figure that is in my mind. You also have to bear in mind what Professor Dunjic did in 2001, sites 1 and 2. I don't know how many bodies were found there. At any rate, we spent six months there from early June until almost the end of December, the 20th or maybe even the 24th of December, that was when we completed our field-work. I can't now recall the exact date. But it's all in the protocols.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Professor, you'll be very pleased to know, I'm sure, that that concludes the questions for you. We have of course your statement and the documents that accompany that which will be studied at some length, and I'm sure we'll learn and hear more about that from counsel in due course. But in the meantime, the Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague, for the work that you've done in this matter over the years, and the assistance you've been able to give us today. We thank you and you may of course now leave at a convenient time to return to your normal activities. The court officer will assist you to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That completes the evidence we anticipated for today. It might be convenient at this moment to return to the question of the two exhibits, Exhibits 97 and 102. You have heard, Ms. Kravetz, the objection of Mr. Djurdjic to your motion for withdrawal of those exhibits. Is there anything you wish to put in response?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to clarify that the only reason we are seeking to withdraw these exhibits is simply because we are at present unable to provide a translation. These exhibits comprise a total of approximately 1.200, 300 pages and CLSS is not able to provide a translation given their current workload in any time soon. These exhibits, although they are relevant to prove the scope of the transfer of bodies from Kosovo to Serbia, they do not relate specifically to any of our scheduled victims; and we have other evidence to prove the scope and the number of bodies transferred. That's the only reason we're seeking to withdraw them, the lack of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Against that, Mr. Djurdjic puts the Defence position that it believes that in time a comparison about the findings of these -- shown in these exhibits and the findings made by the further examination will be an important factual issue for the Chamber when it comes to look at the reports dealing with the actual people, the subject of the indictment. Do you have anything to say in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're interested in having these exhibits in evidence, and if it will assist the Chamber, we have no problem in not withdrawing them. The only thing that I should alert you to is the fact that it will take many months to have the English translation uploaded in e-court. So that is the only issue here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that it -- the position presently ordered should remain, that is, the exhibits P97 and P102 should remain exhibits and subject to the order of the Chamber for translation into English. There seems to be a genuine basis advanced as a matter of fact by the Defence upon which they will seek to rely. Clearly, it's a terrible lot of work involved, and it will take time. It does appear that we will have a little time available. So in those circumstances, Mr. Djurdjic's objection is upheld and will not disturb our existing orders. That, at the surprisingly early stage of today, leads us, I think, to an adjournment because we were not anticipating that we should move today to the next witness. But we will continue the hearing on Wednesday, as we are not able to sit tomorrow, and I believe it's Wednesday afternoon that we are listed to continue. I would mention, in case it has escaped notice, that we are sitting not only Wednesday but Thursday afternoon, but we've been moved to a morning sitting on Friday from what was listed. We now adjourn and we will see you all on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of April, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
